sources_considered.why: Explicit contemporary argument for architectural limitations; evidence of a position, not its prevalence.
Industry acknowledgment of structural mechanisms, coupled with an explicit rejection of inevitability.
Earlier theoretical work establishes that structural explanations predate 2025 and depend on specific assumptions.
Read the abstract. The survey concerns researchers' conceptions of intelligence, which do not directly measure agreement about inherent reliability limits.
Read in full. The planning review documents differing views and hybrid approaches, but does not measure prevalence of the belief claimed.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; Richard Ackermann and Simeon Emanuilov
evidence_items.explanation: This directly expresses the view Marcus describes. One preprint cannot establish widespread acceptance or a recent shift in opinion.

evidence_items.locator: Conclusions, response to the claim that hallucinations are inevitable
evidence_items.explanation: OpenAI discusses statistical causes in training and evaluation, but explicitly rejects inevitable hallucination because models can abstain. Recognition of structural causes therefore cannot automatically be counted as agreement with an unfixable-limit interpretation.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; Adam Tauman Kalai and Santosh S. Vempala
evidence_items.explanation: This earlier paper derives a hallucination bound for particular facts under a calibration condition, while distinguishing other errors that may be mitigated. It establishes prior structural analysis, not prior widespread agreement.

unresolved_gaps: No representative measurement of agreement with the specific inherent-limitations proposition was located.
No comparable earlier and late-2025 measurements establish when recognition became widespread.
The evidence does not establish the separate attribution that industry participants wanted people to regard limitations as temporary bugs.
